SCI-01.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask "unit of X?", "named after whom?", "how many base units?" and quick conversions (light-year, nautical mile, °C to °F). These are easy marks if memorised.

## SI system basics 🔥
- **SI (Système International d'Unités, আন্তর্জাতিক একক পদ্ধতি)** was adopted in **1960** by the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM).
- SI has **7 base units (মৌলিক একক)**. All others are **derived units (লব্ধ একক)**.
- Since **2019 (20 May)**, all 7 base units are defined by fixed physical constants (the kilogram is now defined by the **Planck constant**; earlier it was a platinum-iridium cylinder kept in Sèvres, France).

| Base quantity | SI unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length (দৈর্ঘ্য) | metre | m |
| Mass (ভর) | kilogram | kg |
| Time (সময়) | second | s |
| Temperature (তাপমাত্রা) | kelvin | K |
| Electric current (তড়িৎ প্রবাহ) | ampere | A |
| Luminous intensity (দীপন তীব্রতা) | candela | cd |
| Amount of substance (পদার্থের পরিমাণ) | mole | mol |

**Memory hook:** the seven symbols are **m, kg, s, K, A, cd, mol**. Anything else (N, J, W, Pa, V, Ω) is derived.

## Derived units named after scientists 🔥🔥
| Quantity | Unit | Named after |
|---|---|---|
| Force (বল) | **newton (N)** = kg·m/s² | Isaac Newton |
| Work / energy (কাজ/শক্তি) | **joule (J)** = N·m | James Prescott Joule |
| Power (ক্ষমতা) | **watt (W)** = J/s | James Watt |
| Pressure (চাপ) | **pascal (Pa)** = N/m² | Blaise Pascal |
| Frequency (কম্পাঙ্ক) | **hertz (Hz)** = 1/s | Heinrich Hertz |
| Electric charge (আধান) | **coulomb (C)** = A·s | Charles-Augustin de Coulomb |
| Potential difference (বিভব পার্থক্য) | **volt (V)** | Alessandro Volta |
| Resistance (রোধ) | **ohm (Ω)** | Georg Simon Ohm |
| Capacitance (ধারকত্ব) | **farad (F)** | Michael Faraday |
| Inductance | **henry (H)** | Joseph Henry |
| Magnetic flux | **weber (Wb)** | Wilhelm Weber |
| Magnetic flux density | **tesla (T)** | Nikola Tesla |
| Radioactivity | **becquerel (Bq)** | Henri Becquerel |
| Conductance | **siemens (S)** | Werner von Siemens |
| Absorbed radiation dose | gray (Gy) | Louis Harold Gray |

Other common units: acceleration **m/s²**, velocity **m/s**, density **kg/m³**, momentum **kg·m/s**, work done by electricity (commercial) **kilowatt-hour (kWh)**, 1 kWh = **3.6 × 10⁶ J** (1 "unit" of electricity bill = 1 kWh).

| **Parsec** | Distance | ≈ **3.26 light-years** (largest distance unit commonly asked) |
| **Angstrom (Å)** | Very small length (wavelength) | **10⁻¹⁰ m** |
| **Fermi / femtometre** | Nuclear size | **10⁻¹⁵ m** |
| **Micron (µm)** | Length | 10⁻⁶ m |
| **Nautical mile (নটিক্যাল মাইল)** | Distance at sea | **1,852 m** (≈1.852 km) |
| **Knot** | **Speed of ships** | 1 nautical mile per hour |
| **Mile** | Distance | ≈ 1.609 km |
| **Fathom** | **Depth of sea** | 6 feet (≈1.83 m) |
| **Horsepower (HP)** | Power | **746 W** |
| **Calorie** | Heat energy | **4.2 J** (4.184 J) |
| **Barrel** | Crude oil | ≈ 159 litres |
| **Carat** | Purity of gold (24 carat = pure) / mass of gems (1 carat = 200 mg) | |
| **Decibel (dB)** | Sound intensity level | |

| **Hectare** | Land area | 10,000 m² (≈ 2.47 acres) |

- 1 atmosphere (standard pressure) = **1.013 × 10⁵ Pa** = **76 cm (760 mm) of mercury**.
- 1 acre ≈ 100 decimal (শতাংশ); 1 bigha (Bangladesh) = 33 decimal (common value).

## Prefixes

|---|---|---|---|
| kilo (k) | 10³ | milli (m) | 10⁻³ |
| mega (M) | 10⁶ | micro (µ) | 10⁻⁶ |

| tera (T) | 10¹² | pico (p) | 10⁻¹² |
| peta (P) | 10¹⁵ | femto (f) | 10⁻¹⁵ |

## Temperature scales 🔥
- Formula: **C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5**.
- Water freezes: **0 °C = 32 °F = 273 K**. Water boils: **100 °C = 212 °F = 373 K**.
- **−40 °C = −40 °F** (the two scales are equal at −40).
- Normal human body temperature: **37 °C = 98.4–98.6 °F** (NCTB uses 98.4 °F; many guides say 98.6 °F).

| **Screw gauge** | Diameter of thin wire |
| **Barometer** | **Atmospheric pressure** (Torricelli) |

## Quick revision
- SI adopted 1960; **7 base units**; kilogram redefined by Planck constant in 2019.
- Unit of force **newton**, work **joule**, power **watt**, pressure **pascal**.
- **Light-year is a unit of distance**, ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.
- **1 HP = 746 W**; **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J**.
- **1 nautical mile = 1,852 m**; knot = speed of ships.
- **1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m**; fermi = 10⁻¹⁵ m.
- **−40 °C = −40 °F**; body temperature 37 °C.
- Lactometer: milk; hygrometer: humidity; anemometer: wind speed.

SCI-02.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask which Newton's law explains an everyday event, the value of g, escape velocity, where weight is greatest/least, and scalar vs vector quantities.

## Scalar and vector (স্কেলার ও ভেক্টর রাশি) 🔥
| Scalar (magnitude only) | Vector (magnitude + direction) |
|---|---|
| Mass, distance, speed, time, work, energy, power, temperature, density, electric current | **Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum**, torque, electric field |

- **Speed (দ্রুতি)** = distance/time (scalar). **Velocity (বেগ)** = displacement/time (vector).
- **Acceleration (ত্বরণ)** = rate of change of velocity, unit **m/s²**.
- Equations of motion (uniform acceleration): **v = u + at**, **s = ut + ½at²**, **v² = u² + 2as**.

## Newton's laws of motion 🔥🔥
Isaac Newton published them in ***Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687)**.

| Law | Statement | Everyday examples |
|---|---|---|
| **1st law (law of inertia, জড়তার সূত্র)** | A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts on it | Passengers fall **backward when a bus suddenly starts** and **forward when it suddenly stops**; dust leaves a carpet when beaten |
| **2nd law** | Rate of change of momentum ∝ applied force; **F = ma** | Cricketer pulls hands back while catching (more time, less force); defines the unit of force |
| **3rd law** | **Every action has an equal and opposite reaction** | **Rocket and jet propulsion**, gun **recoil**, swimming, walking, a boat moving back when you jump ashore |

- **Inertia (জড়তা)**: tendency to resist change of state. **Mass is the measure of inertia.** Two types: inertia of rest, inertia of motion. Galileo first described it.
- **Momentum (ভরবেগ)** p = mv, unit kg·m/s. **Law of conservation of momentum** explains rocket motion and gun recoil.
- **1 newton** = force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². 1 kg-wt ≈ 9.8 N.

## Friction and circular motion
- **Friction (ঘর্ষণ)** opposes motion. Static friction > sliding friction > rolling friction. That is why **ball bearings / wheels** reduce friction. Lubricants (oil, grease) also reduce it.
- Friction is needed for walking and for brakes; we slip on ice/banana peel because friction is low.
- **Centripetal force (কেন্দ্রমুখী বল)** keeps a body in circular motion, directed toward the centre. Roads and railway tracks are **banked** at curves to provide it. A cyclist leans inward on a turn.
- A **washing-machine dryer / cream separator** works on the "centrifugal" effect.

## Gravitation (মহাকর্ষ ও অভিকর্ষ) 🔥
- **Newton's law of universal gravitation**: F = G m₁m₂ / d². Force ∝ product of masses, ∝ 1/(distance)².
- **G (universal gravitational constant) = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²**; it is the same everywhere. It was first measured by **Henry Cavendish (1798)**.
- **Gravity (অভিকর্ষ)** = Earth's pull on a body. **g (acceleration due to gravity) ≈ 9.8 m/s²** (9.81) at Earth's surface.
- **Mass (ভর)** is constant everywhere; **weight (ওজন) = mg** changes with g. Weight is a force (unit N); mass unit kg.

| Where | Value of g / weight |
|---|---|
| **Poles (মেরু)** | **Maximum** g (Earth is flattened at poles, radius smaller) |
| **Equator (বিষুবরেখা)** | **Minimum** g on the surface |
| **Centre of the Earth** | **g = 0**, weight zero |
| Going up (height) or down (depth) | g decreases |
| **Moon** | g ≈ **1/6** of Earth's → weight on Moon is **1/6** of that on Earth; mass is the same |
| Freely falling lift / orbiting spacecraft | **Weightlessness (ওজনহীনতা)** |

- **Galileo**: in vacuum, all bodies fall with the **same acceleration** regardless of mass (a feather and a coin fall together in vacuum). He is said to have tested it at the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
- Lift going **up with acceleration** → apparent weight increases; **going down with acceleration** → decreases; **free fall** → zero.

## Escape velocity and satellites 🔥
| Term | Value |
|---|---|
| **Escape velocity (মুক্তিবেগ) of Earth** | **11.2 km/s** |
| Escape velocity of Moon | ≈ 2.4 km/s (that is why the Moon has no atmosphere) |
| **Orbital velocity** near Earth's surface | ≈ **7.9 km/s** (≈ 8 km/s) |
| **Geostationary (ভূস্থির) satellite** height | ≈ **36,000 km** (35,786 km) above the equator; period **24 hours**; used for communication and TV. **Bangabandhu Satellite-1** (launched 12 May 2018) is geostationary at **119.1° E** |

## Kepler's laws of planetary motion
Johannes **Kepler** (1609–1619):
1. Planets move in **elliptical orbits** with the Sun at one **focus**.
2. The line joining planet and Sun sweeps **equal areas in equal times** (planet moves faster near the Sun).
3. **T² ∝ r³** (square of the period ∝ cube of mean distance).

## Pressure and floating (quick facts)
- **Pascal's law** → hydraulic press, hydraulic brake, hydraulic lift.
- **Archimedes' principle** → buoyancy; a floating body displaces its own weight of liquid (law of floatation). Ships float, ice floats (ice density < water).
- **Bernoulli's principle** → aeroplane lift, atomizer/sprayer.

## Quick revision
- Newton's 1st law = **law of inertia**; mass measures inertia.
- **F = ma** (2nd law); **rocket works on the 3rd law** / conservation of momentum.
- **g = 9.8 m/s²**; G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² (Cavendish).
- g is **maximum at the poles**, minimum at the equator, **zero at Earth's centre**.
- Weight on the Moon is **1/6** of Earth weight; mass remains same.
- **Escape velocity 11.2 km/s**; geostationary satellite ≈ 36,000 km, period 24 h.
- Velocity, force, momentum, displacement are vectors; speed, mass, work are scalars.

SCI-03.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask units (joule, watt, kWh, HP), energy conversions in devices, "when is work zero?", and simple calculations of kinetic energy and power.

## Work (কাজ) 🔥
- **Work = Force × displacement in the direction of force**: **W = F s cos θ**.
- Unit: **joule (J)** = 1 N × 1 m. Work is a **scalar**. Dimension: ML²T⁻².
- **Work is zero** when:
  - there is **no displacement** (pushing a wall, holding a heavy load while standing still);
  - force is **perpendicular** to displacement (θ = 90°): carrying a load on the head while walking on level ground; the Moon going round the Earth (centripetal force ⟂ motion).
- **Negative work**: friction on a moving body; work done by gravity on a body thrown upward.
- Other work/energy units: **1 erg = 10⁻⁷ J** (CGS); **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J**; **1 calorie ≈ 4.2 J**; 1 electron-volt (eV) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

## Energy (শক্তি) 🔥
Energy is the **capacity to do work**. Unit is the same as work: **joule**.

| Form | Formula / fact |
|---|---|
| **Kinetic energy (গতিশক্তি)** | **KE = ½ mv²**. Doubling speed → KE becomes **4 times** |
| **Potential energy (বিভবশক্তি)** | **PE = mgh** (gravitational). Also stored in a stretched spring, wound watch-spring, water in a dam |
| Others | Heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical, nuclear, magnetic energy |

- **Law of conservation of energy (শক্তির নিত্যতা সূত্র):** energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes form. Total energy of the universe is constant.
- **Einstein's mass–energy relation: E = mc²** (1905) — mass can be converted into energy (basis of nuclear energy).
- A freely falling body: PE decreases, KE increases, total (PE + KE) stays constant.
- **Main source of energy on Earth: the Sun**. The Sun's energy comes from **nuclear fusion**.

## Energy conversions in devices 🔥
| Device | Conversion |
|---|---|
| **Electric motor / fan** | Electrical → **mechanical** |
| **Generator / dynamo** | **Mechanical → electrical** |
| Electric bulb | Electrical → light (+ heat) |
| Electric heater / iron | Electrical → heat |
| **Battery / cell (discharging)** | **Chemical → electrical** |
| Storage battery (charging) | Electrical → chemical |
| **Solar cell** | **Light (solar) → electrical** |
| Microphone | Sound → electrical |
| Loudspeaker | Electrical → sound |
| Steam engine / car engine | Heat (chemical) → mechanical |
| Photosynthesis | Light → chemical |
| Hydroelectric plant (Kaptai) | Potential energy of water → kinetic → electrical |
| Nuclear reactor | Nuclear → heat → electrical |

## Power (ক্ষমতা) 🔥
- **Power = work done per unit time**: **P = W/t**. It measures the **rate** of doing work.
- Unit: **watt (W) = 1 J/s** (after James Watt, improver of the steam engine).
- **1 horsepower (HP) = 746 W** (the term HP was coined by James Watt).
- 1 kW = 1,000 W; 1 MW = 10⁶ W.
- **kilowatt-hour (kWh)** is a unit of **energy**, not power. The "unit" on an electricity bill = **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ**.
- Electrical power: **P = VI = I²R = V²/R**.

### Worked examples
1. A 1,000 W heater runs for 2 hours. Energy used? → 1 kW × 2 h = **2 kWh (2 units)**.
2. A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. KE? → ½ × 2 × 3² = **9 J**.
3. A 10 kg load is raised 5 m (g = 9.8). PE? → 10 × 9.8 × 5 = **490 J**.
4. A 60 W bulb burns 5 hours a day for 30 days. Units? → 60 × 5 × 30 = 9,000 Wh = **9 kWh**.

## Efficiency (কর্মদক্ষতা)
- **Efficiency = (useful output ÷ input) × 100%**. It is always **less than 100%** in real machines because of friction and heat loss.
- Simple machines (lever, pulley, inclined plane, screw, wedge, wheel and axle) give **mechanical advantage**; they do not reduce total work.
- Levers: **1st class** — fulcrum in middle (scissors, see-saw, pliers); **2nd class** — load in middle (nutcracker, wheelbarrow); **3rd class** — effort in middle (forceps/tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm).

## Quick revision
- Unit of work and energy: **joule**; unit of power: **watt**.
- **1 HP = 746 W**; **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J** (unit of energy).
- **KE = ½mv²**, **PE = mgh**; double speed → 4 times KE.
- Pushing a wall or carrying a load on level ground → **work done = 0** (in physics).
- **E = mc²** (Einstein, 1905).
- **Generator: mechanical → electrical; motor: electrical → mechanical.**
- **Battery: chemical → electrical**; solar cell: light → electrical.
- Nutcracker = 2nd class lever; forceps = 3rd class lever.

SCI-04.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask heat vs temperature, units, absolute zero, the 4 °C anomaly of water, modes of heat transfer with examples, and why a pressure cooker cooks faster.

## Heat vs temperature 🔥
| Heat (তাপ) | Temperature (তাপমাত্রা) |
|---|---|
| A **form of energy**; total kinetic energy of molecules | **Degree of hotness**; average kinetic energy of molecules |
| Unit **joule (J)**; also calorie (1 cal ≈ 4.2 J) | SI unit **kelvin (K)**; also °C, °F |
| Measured by a **calorimeter** | Measured by a **thermometer** |
| Cause | Effect |

- Heat flows from **higher to lower temperature**, not from more heat to less heat.
- Joule showed that heat is a form of energy (mechanical equivalent of heat, J ≈ 4.2 J/cal).

## Temperature scales and thermometers 🔥
- **C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5**.
- **Absolute zero (পরম শূন্য) = 0 K = −273.15 °C (≈ −273 °C) = −459.67 °F**. At absolute zero molecular motion is (theoretically) minimum.
- **Kelvin scale** was given by **Lord Kelvin (William Thomson)**; it has no negative values.
- **−40 °C = −40 °F**. Body temperature **37 °C = 98.4 °F (NCTB) / 98.6 °F = 310 K**.

| Thermometer | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Clinical thermometer** | Range **35–42 °C (95–110 °F)**; has a **kink (constriction)** so mercury doesn't fall back |
| **Mercury thermometer** | Mercury freezes at **−39 °C**, boils at **357 °C**; shiny, uniform expansion, doesn't wet glass. Fahrenheit made it (1714) |
| **Alcohol thermometer** | For **very low temperatures** (alcohol freezes near −115 °C), e.g. polar regions |
| **Pyrometer** | **Very high temperature** (furnaces, Sun) — works by radiation |
| **Thermocouple** | Wide range, uses Seebeck effect |
| Galileo | Made the first thermometer (air thermoscope, c. 1593) |

## Specific heat and latent heat 🔥
- **Specific heat (আপেক্ষিক তাপ)**: heat needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K. Water: **4,200 J/kg·K** (1 cal/g·°C) — **highest among common substances**. So water is used in radiators and hot-water bags, and the sea heats and cools slowly (mild coastal climate).
- **Q = m s Δt** (heat = mass × specific heat × change in temperature).
- **Latent heat (সুপ্ত তাপ)**: heat absorbed/released during change of state **without change of temperature**.
  - Latent heat of **fusion of ice = 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg (80 cal/g)**.
  - Latent heat of **vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg (≈540 cal/g)**. That is why **steam at 100 °C burns more severely than boiling water at 100 °C**.

## Anomalous expansion of water 🔥
- Water has **maximum density (minimum volume) at 4 °C**.
- From 0 °C to 4 °C water **contracts** on heating; above 4 °C it expands.
- Result: in cold countries lakes freeze **from the top**, water at 4 °C stays at the bottom and **fish survive**. Water pipes burst in winter because water expands on freezing. Ice floats (ice is less dense than water, about 0.92 g/cm³).

## Transfer of heat (তাপ সঞ্চালন) 🔥
| Mode | How | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Conduction (পরিবহন)** | Molecule to molecule, **no bulk movement**; mainly in **solids** | Metal spoon gets hot; cooking pots of metal with wooden/plastic handles. **Silver is the best conductor of heat**, then copper |
| **Convection (পরিচলন)** | **Movement of the heated fluid itself**; liquids and gases | **Sea breeze (day) and land breeze (night)**, boiling water, ventilators placed high, trade winds |
| **Radiation (বিকিরণ)** | **Needs no medium**; travels as electromagnetic (infrared) waves at the speed of light | **Sun's heat reaches Earth**; heat felt near a fire |

- **Thermos (vacuum) flask**, invented by **James Dewar** (1892): vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered walls stop radiation.
- **Black, rough surfaces absorb and emit heat best**; white/shiny surfaces reflect. So **white clothes are cooler in summer**, dark clothes warmer in winter.
- Bad conductors (insulators): wood, air, wool, glass, plastic. Woollen clothes keep us warm because they **trap air**, a bad conductor.

## Boiling, melting and pressure 🔥
- Water boils at **100 °C at 1 atm**. **Boiling point rises with pressure** → a **pressure cooker** cooks faster (about 120 °C inside). Papin invented it ("Papin's digester").
- At **high altitude** (mountains) pressure is low, so water boils **below 100 °C** and food cooks slowly.
- **Impurities (salt) raise the boiling point** and **lower the freezing point** (salt is spread on icy roads; ice-salt mixture for ice cream).
- **Melting point of ice falls with pressure** → **regelation**; ice skating.
- **Evaporation (বাষ্পীভবন) causes cooling**: sweating, water in an earthen pot (কলসি) stays cool, we feel cold after spirit/acetone on skin. Evaporation happens at any temperature, only at the surface.
- **Dew point (শিশিরাঙ্ক)**: the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapour condenses as dew.

## Thermal expansion
- Gaps are left between **railway rails** and in bridges; telephone/electric wires **sag in summer**.
- **Bimetallic strip** (e.g. brass + iron) bends on heating → used in **thermostats**, fire alarms, electric irons.
- **Invar** (iron-nickel alloy) has very low expansion → pendulum clocks, measuring tapes.

## Quick revision
- Heat is energy (J); temperature is degree of hotness (K).
- **Absolute zero = 0 K = −273 °C**; −40 °C = −40 °F.
- Water: **maximum density at 4 °C**; specific heat **4,200 J/kg·K** (highest common).
- **Steam burns more** than boiling water (latent heat of vaporisation).
- **Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation**; sea/land breeze by **convection**.
- **Pressure cooker**: higher pressure → higher boiling point.
- Clinical thermometer 35–42 °C; alcohol for low, pyrometer for very high temperature.
- Thermos flask: James Dewar.

SCI-05.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the speed of sound in different media, audible range, ultrasonic/infrasonic uses, echo distance, unit of loudness and the Doppler effect.

## Nature of sound 🔥
- Sound is a form of energy produced by **vibration (কম্পন)**.
- Sound needs a **material medium**; it **cannot travel through a vacuum**. So astronauts on the Moon talk by radio (radio waves are electromagnetic).
- In air (and other fluids) sound travels as a **longitudinal wave (অনুদৈর্ঘ্য তরঙ্গ)** — compressions and rarefactions. In solids it can be both longitudinal and transverse. (Light, by contrast, is a transverse electromagnetic wave.)
- **Wave equation: v = f λ** (speed = frequency × wavelength). Frequency unit: **hertz (Hz)**.

## Speed of sound 🔥🔥
| Medium | Approx. speed |
|---|---|
| **Air at 0 °C** | **332 m/s** (NCTB value; many books say 330–332 m/s) |
| Air at about 20 °C | ≈ 343 m/s |
| **Water** | ≈ **1,450–1,500 m/s** (about 4 times air) |
| **Iron / steel** | ≈ **5,000–5,200 m/s** (about 15 times air) |

- Order: **solid > liquid > gas**. Speed is **zero in vacuum**.
- Speed in air **increases with temperature** (about **0.6 m/s per °C**) and with **humidity** (sound travels faster in moist air, so faster in the rainy season).
- Change of **pressure alone does not change** the speed of sound (at constant temperature).
- **Light is much faster** (3 × 10⁸ m/s), so we **see lightning before hearing thunder**.
- **Supersonic (শব্দোত্তর)**: faster than sound. **Mach number** = speed of object ÷ speed of sound (Mach 1 = speed of sound). A supersonic jet produces a **sonic boom**.

## Frequency ranges 🔥
| Type | Frequency | Examples / uses |
|---|---|---|
| **Infrasonic (শব্দেতর)** | **Below 20 Hz** | Produced by **earthquakes**, volcanoes; heard by **elephants, whales**, dogs sense some |
| **Audible (শ্রাব্যতার সীমা)** | **20 Hz – 20,000 Hz** | Human hearing |
| **Ultrasonic (শব্দোত্তর/অতিস্বনক)** | **Above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)** | **Bats (echolocation), dolphins**; **SONAR**, **ultrasonography** (seeing a fetus), cleaning delicate parts, detecting flaws in metal, kidney-stone breaking |

- **SONAR = Sound Navigation And Ranging** — uses ultrasound to find sea depth, submarines, fish shoals.
- **Bats** fly in darkness by emitting ultrasound and hearing its echo.
- Dogs can hear up to about 40–45 kHz (dog whistles are ultrasonic to humans).

## Characteristics of sound 🔥
| Characteristic | Depends on |
|---|---|
| **Pitch (তীক্ষ্ণতা)** — shrillness | **Frequency**. Women's and children's voices have **higher pitch** than men's; a mosquito's buzz has higher pitch than a lion's roar |
| **Loudness / intensity (প্রাবল্য/তীব্রতা)** | **Amplitude**; also distance and area of vibrating body |
| **Quality / timbre (স্বরের গুণ)** | **Overtones / harmonics** (waveform); lets us recognise a voice or instrument |

- **Loudness unit: decibel (dB)**; the bel is named after **Alexander Graham Bell**. 0 dB ≈ threshold of hearing; normal talk ≈ 60 dB. Prolonged exposure above about **85 dB** can damage hearing; above ~120 dB is painful.
- Sound above a comfortable level is **noise (শব্দদূষণ)**; the loudness of noise is measured in dB with a sound-level meter.

## Echo and reverberation 🔥
- **Echo (প্রতিধ্বনি)**: reflected sound heard separately. The effect of a sound stays in our ear for about **0.1 s** (persistence of hearing).
- So the reflecting surface must be at least **≈ 16.6 m (about 17 m) away** in air (332 × 0.1 ÷ 2).
- Echo formula: **distance = (speed × time) ÷ 2**.
  - *Example:* echo heard after 2 s, speed 332 m/s → d = 332 × 2 ÷ 2 = **332 m**.
- **Reverberation**: many overlapping reflections in a hall; reduced with curtains, soft boards, carpets.
- Uses of reflection of sound: stethoscope, megaphone, whispering galleries, sound boards, ear trumpets.

## Other effects
- **Doppler effect** (Christian **Doppler**, 1842): apparent change of frequency when source and listener move relative to each other. The horn of an approaching train sounds **higher**, of a receding train **lower**. Also used in police radar and to find the speed of stars (red shift).
- **Resonance (অনুনাদ)**: large vibration when forced frequency = natural frequency. Soldiers **break step while crossing a bridge**; tuning a radio uses resonance.
- **Stethoscope** was invented by **René Laennec (1816)**; it works by multiple reflection of sound.
- Musical instruments: string (violin, sitar), wind (flute), percussion (drum, tabla).

## Quick revision
- Sound **cannot travel in vacuum**; it is a **longitudinal** wave in air.
- Speed in air ≈ **332 m/s at 0 °C**; **solid > liquid > gas**.
- Speed rises with **temperature and humidity**, not with pressure alone.
- **Audible range 20 Hz – 20 kHz**; above = ultrasonic, below = infrasonic.
- Bats and SONAR use **ultrasound**; earthquakes produce **infrasound**.
- **Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude; quality ↔ overtones**.
- Echo needs at least **≈17 m**; loudness unit **decibel**.
- Approaching train horn sounds higher: **Doppler effect**.

SCI-06.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the speed of light, which mirror/lens is used where, eye defects and their correction, why the sky is blue, how a rainbow forms and total internal reflection examples.

## Nature and speed of light 🔥
- Light is an **electromagnetic, transverse wave**; it has a **dual nature** (wave and particle/photon). Photon idea: Einstein's **photoelectric effect** (Nobel 1921).
- **Speed in vacuum ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s** (3 lakh km/s). It is slower in water (≈2.25 × 10⁸) and glass (≈2 × 10⁸).
- **Sunlight reaches Earth in ≈ 8 minutes 20 seconds (≈500 s)**. Moonlight reaches in ≈ 1.3 s.
- Visible light wavelength: about **400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red)** (some books: 3.9 × 10⁻⁷ – 7.8 × 10⁻⁷ m).
- Light travels in a **straight line** → shadows, eclipses, **pinhole camera** (image real and inverted).

## Reflection (প্রতিফলন) 🔥
- **Laws:** (1) angle of incidence = angle of reflection; (2) incident ray, reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane.
- **Plane mirror image:** **virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted** (left ↔ right), as far behind as the object is in front. To see your full body you need a mirror of at least **half your height**.
- Two plane mirrors at angle θ → number of images = **(360/θ) − 1** (e.g. 90° → 3 images; parallel mirrors → infinite images).
- **Periscope** uses two plane mirrors (at 45°); **kaleidoscope** uses multiple reflection.

| Mirror | Uses |
|---|---|
| **Concave (অবতল) — converging** | **Shaving/make-up mirror**, **dentist's mirror**, **reflectors of torch, car headlight, searchlight**, solar cooker, reflecting telescope |
| **Convex (উত্তল) — diverging** | **Rear-view (side) mirror of vehicles** (gives a wide field of view; image virtual, erect, diminished), street-corner mirrors |

## Refraction (প্রতিসরণ) 🔥
- Bending of light when it passes from one medium to another because its **speed changes**.
- **Snell's law:** sin i / sin r = constant (**refractive index, μ**). **μ = speed in vacuum ÷ speed in medium**.
- Refractive index: water **1.33**, glass **1.5**, **diamond 2.42** (very high).
- Everyday effects: **a stick looks bent in water**; **a pond looks shallower** and a coin in water appears raised; **stars twinkle** (atmospheric refraction); the Sun is visible a little **before actual sunrise and after sunset**.

### Total internal reflection (পূর্ণ অভ্যন্তরীণ প্রতিফলন) 🔥
- Occurs when light goes from a **denser to a rarer medium** and the angle of incidence **exceeds the critical angle** (glass ≈ 42°, diamond ≈ 24°).
- Examples: **sparkling of diamond**, **mirage (মরীচিকা)** in deserts / hot roads, **optical fibre** (used in telecommunication and **endoscopy**), a glass crack appearing silvery. Optical fibre pioneer: **Narinder Singh Kapany** (often called the father of fibre optics).

## Lenses (লেন্স) 🔥
| Lens | Nature | Power sign | Uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Convex (উত্তল)** | Converging, thick in middle | **+** | **Magnifying glass**, camera, projector, microscope, telescope; corrects **long-sightedness (hypermetropia)** |
| **Concave (অবতল)** | Diverging, thin in middle | **−** | Corrects **short-sightedness (myopia)**; peep-hole of doors |

- **Power of a lens (P) = 1/f**, f in metres; unit **dioptre (D)**. A lens of f = +50 cm has P = +2 D.
- A convex lens in water loses much of its power; an air bubble in water acts as a **concave lens**.

## The human eye and its defects 🔥
- Eye lens is **convex**; image on the **retina** is **real and inverted**; the brain makes it upright.
- **Rods** work in dim light; **cones** detect **colour**. **Iris** controls pupil size. **Near point ≈ 25 cm**; far point = infinity.
- **Persistence of vision ≈ 1/16 s (≈0.1 s)** → basis of cinema.

| Defect | Problem | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| **Myopia (হ্রস্বদৃষ্টি)** | Can't see **far**; image forms in front of retina | **Concave lens** |
| **Hypermetropia (দীর্ঘদৃষ্টি)** | Can't see **near**; image behind retina | **Convex lens** |
| **Presbyopia (চালশে)** | Old age; weak accommodation | **Bifocal lens** (invented by **Benjamin Franklin**) |
| **Astigmatism** | Uneven cornea; blurred in some directions | **Cylindrical lens** |
| **Cataract (ছানি)** | Lens becomes cloudy | Surgery / artificial lens |

## Dispersion, scattering and colour 🔥
- **Dispersion (বিচ্ছুরণ):** white light splits into 7 colours through a **prism** — shown by **Isaac Newton (1666)**. Order **VIBGYOR** (বেনীআসহকলা): Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.
- **Red**: longest wavelength, **least deviation**, least scattering. **Violet**: shortest wavelength, **most deviation**.
- **Rainbow (রংধনু)**: formed by **dispersion + refraction + total internal reflection** in raindrops; seen in the sky **opposite the Sun**; red on the outer side (primary bow).
- **Scattering (বিক্ষেপণ)** (Rayleigh; scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴): **sky is blue**; **Sun looks red at sunrise/sunset**; **danger signals are red** (least scattered, seen from far); the sky looks **black to astronauts** in space (no air to scatter light).
- **Raman effect**: C. V. Raman (Nobel Prize in Physics, **1930**) — change in wavelength of scattered light.
- **Primary colours of light: red, green, blue**. Red + green + blue = white. **Complementary pairs**: red–cyan, green–magenta, blue–yellow.
- An object looks red because it **reflects red and absorbs others**; a red rose in green light looks **black**.

## Quick revision
- Speed of light **3 × 10⁸ m/s**; sunlight takes **≈8 min 20 s**.
- Rear-view mirror = **convex**; shaving mirror & headlight reflector = **concave**.
- Myopia → **concave lens**; hypermetropia → **convex lens**; bifocal → Franklin.
- Diamond sparkles & optical fibre work by **total internal reflection**; mirage too.
- **Sky blue, sunset red**: scattering; danger signal red.
- **VIBGYOR**; red least deviated, violet most.
- Power of lens in **dioptre**, P = 1/f (m).
- Raman effect (1930 Nobel); dispersion by Newton.

SCI-07.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask Ohm's law, units, which metal/alloy is used in filament, heater and fuse, household supply (220 V, 50 Hz), AC/DC, transformer and generator principles, and magnetic materials.

## Charge and current 🔥
- **Charge (আধান)** unit **coulomb (C)**. Charge of one electron = **−1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C**. Like charges repel, unlike attract (**Coulomb's law**: F ∝ q₁q₂/r²).
- **Current (তড়িৎ প্রবাহ)** I = Q/t, unit **ampere (A)**. Conventional current flows from + to −; **electrons flow from − to +**.
- **Potential difference (বিভব পার্থক্য)** unit **volt (V)**; measured by a **voltmeter (connected in parallel)**. Current is measured by an **ammeter (connected in series)**. A **galvanometer** detects small currents.

## Ohm's law and resistance 🔥🔥
- **Ohm's law** (Georg Simon **Ohm**, 1827): at constant temperature, **V = IR**.
- **Resistance (রোধ)** unit **ohm (Ω)**. R = ρL/A — increases with **length**, decreases with **cross-sectional area**, depends on **material** and **temperature** (for metals it rises with temperature).
- **Series:** R = R₁ + R₂ + … (same current). **Parallel:** 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same voltage; total resistance smaller).
- **Household wiring is in parallel**, so each appliance gets full voltage and works independently.
- Electrical power **P = VI = I²R = V²/R**; energy in **kWh** (1 unit).

| Material | Type / use |
|---|---|
| **Silver** | **Best conductor** of electricity (and heat) |
| **Copper**, aluminium | Wires and cables (copper cheaper than silver) |
| **Tungsten** | **Bulb filament** — very high melting point (≈ 3,400 °C) |
| **Nichrome** (Ni + Cr) | **Heater / iron coil** — high resistance, doesn't oxidise |
| **Fuse wire: tin + lead alloy** | **Low melting point**; placed **in series in the live wire**; melts when current is excessive |
| Rubber, glass, plastic, dry wood, mica | **Insulators** (অন্তরক) |
| **Silicon (Si), germanium (Ge)** | **Semiconductors** — diode, transistor, IC, solar cell |
| Superconductor | **Zero resistance** at very low temperature (discovered by **Kamerlingh Onnes, 1911**, in mercury) |

- A bulb is filled with an **inert gas (argon/nitrogen)** so the filament does not burn/evaporate quickly.
- **Semiconductor doping**: adding pentavalent impurity (P, As) → **n-type**; trivalent (B, Al, Ga) → **p-type**.
- **Diode** acts as a **rectifier (AC → DC)**. **Transistor** (1947, Bell Labs: **Bardeen, Brattain, Shockley**) amplifies and switches.

## Cells and batteries 🔥
| Cell | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Voltaic pile** | First battery, **Alessandro Volta (1800)** |
| **Dry cell (Leclanché)** | Zinc case (−), **carbon rod (+)**, MnO₂ and **ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl)** paste; **1.5 V** |
| **Lead-acid (storage) battery** | Car/IPS battery; electrolyte **dilute sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)**; **2 V per cell** (12 V battery = 6 cells); rechargeable |
| **Lithium-ion** | Mobile phones, laptops, EVs (Nobel Chemistry 2019: Goodenough, Whittingham, Yoshino) |

- A battery converts **chemical energy → electrical energy** and gives **DC**.

## AC, DC and supply in Bangladesh 🔥
- **DC (direct current)**: flows one way (battery, solar panel). **AC (alternating current)**: changes direction periodically (power grid).
- **Bangladesh household supply: 220 V, 50 Hz AC** (USA: 110–120 V, 60 Hz).
- **Transformer** changes AC voltage (**step-up / step-down**); works **only on AC**, on the principle of **mutual induction**. Power is transmitted at **high voltage** to reduce loss (I²R).
- **Earthing**: the earth wire (green / green-yellow) protects against shock. A **circuit breaker** also protects circuits.
- **Lightning conductor** was invented by **Benjamin Franklin** (he also showed lightning is electricity, kite experiment, 1752).

## Electromagnetism 🔥
| Discovery | Scientist |
|---|---|
| **Current produces a magnetic field** (1820) | **Hans Christian Oersted** |
| **Electromagnetic induction** (1831) — basis of **generator/dynamo** and transformer | **Michael Faraday** |
| Direction of induced current (Lenz's law) | Heinrich Lenz |
| Electromagnetic theory of light | James Clerk Maxwell |
| Motor rule / generator rule | Fleming's **left-hand rule (motor)**, **right-hand rule (generator)** |

- **Generator**: mechanical → electrical (electromagnetic induction). **Motor**: electrical → mechanical.
- **Electromagnet**: coil around a **soft iron** core; magnetism lasts only while current flows. Used in electric bells, cranes, relays, MRI, loudspeakers.

## Magnetism (চুম্বকত্ব)
- **Natural magnet: magnetite / lodestone (Fe₃O₄)**.
- **Ferromagnetic (strongly attracted)**: **iron, cobalt, nickel** (and their alloys). Copper, gold, wood are non-magnetic.
- **Permanent magnets**: **steel, alnico** (Al-Ni-Co), neodymium magnets. **Temporary**: soft iron.
- Like poles repel, unlike attract; **repulsion is the sure test** of a magnet.
- A freely suspended magnet (compass) points **north–south**. The Earth behaves like a giant magnet; Earth's magnetic poles are not exactly at the geographic poles (angle between them = **declination**).
- Heating above the **Curie temperature** destroys ferromagnetism; hammering also weakens a magnet.
- Units: magnetic flux **weber (Wb)**; magnetic flux density **tesla (T)**.
- **Maglev trains** use magnetic levitation.

## Quick revision
- **V = IR** (Ohm); unit of resistance ohm, of current ampere.
- Filament **tungsten**; heater **nichrome**; fuse **tin–lead** (low melting point), in series.
- **Silver** is the best conductor; **copper** used in wiring.
- Bangladesh supply: **220 V, 50 Hz AC**; house wiring in **parallel**.
- **Transformer works only on AC**; generator: **Faraday's electromagnetic induction** (1831).
- Dry cell **1.5 V**; lead-acid cell **2 V** with dilute H₂SO₄.
- Oersted: current → magnetism (1820); Franklin: lightning conductor.
- Iron, cobalt, nickel are ferromagnetic; natural magnet = magnetite (Fe₃O₄).

SCI-08.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask who discovered radioactivity and the subatomic particles, properties of α, β, γ rays, fission vs fusion (atom bomb vs hydrogen bomb vs the Sun), parts of a nuclear reactor, uses of isotopes and Rooppur facts.

## The nucleus and its particles 🔥
| Particle | Charge | Discovered by |
|---|---|---|
| **Electron** | −1 | **J. J. Thomson (1897)** (cathode rays) |
| **Proton** | +1 | **Ernest Rutherford** (1919; Goldstein saw anode/canal rays in 1886) |
| **Neutron** | 0 | **James Chadwick (1932)** |
| **Nucleus** | + | **Rutherford (1911)**, gold-foil (α-scattering) experiment |

- **Atomic number (Z)** = number of protons. **Mass number (A)** = protons + neutrons.
- **Isotopes (আইসোটোপ)**: same Z, different A (term by **Frederick Soddy**). Hydrogen has 3: **protium (¹H), deuterium (²H, D), tritium (³H, radioactive)**. **Heavy water = D₂O** (deuterium found by Harold Urey, 1931).
- **Isobars**: same A, different Z (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰Ca). **Isotones**: same number of neutrons.
- **Satyendra Nath Bose** (Dhaka University) developed Bose–Einstein statistics (1924); particles called **bosons** are named after him. The **Higgs boson** ("God particle") was confirmed at **CERN in 2012**.

## Radioactivity (তেজস্ক্রিয়তা) 🔥🔥
- Discovered by **Henri Becquerel (1896)** in **uranium** salts.
- **Marie and Pierre Curie** discovered **polonium and radium (1898)**; Marie Curie coined the word "radioactivity" and won Nobel Prizes in **Physics (1903)** and **Chemistry (1911)**.
- Radioactivity is a **nuclear** property; it is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination.
- Elements with Z > 82 (after lead/bismuth) are generally radioactive; e.g. **uranium, thorium, radium, plutonium**.

| Ray | Nature | Charge | Penetrating power | Ionising power |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Alpha (α)** | **Helium nucleus (⁴₂He)** | +2 | **Least** (stopped by paper) | **Most** |
| **Beta (β)** | Fast **electron** | −1 | Medium (stopped by thin aluminium) | Medium |
| **Gamma (γ)** | **Electromagnetic wave** (photon) | **0** | **Most** (needs thick **lead**/concrete) | Least |

- α and β were named by **Rutherford**; γ rays were discovered by **Paul Villard (1900)**. γ rays are **not deflected** by electric or magnetic fields.
- **Half-life (অর্ধায়ু)**: time for half the nuclei to decay. **Carbon-14: ≈ 5,730 years** → **radiocarbon dating** of fossils and old wood (developed by **Willard Libby**).
- Units: **becquerel (Bq)** (SI) = 1 decay/s; **curie (Ci) = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq**. Radiation dose: sievert (Sv), gray (Gy). Detector: **Geiger–Müller counter**.

## Uses of radioisotopes 🔥
| Isotope | Use |
|---|---|
| **Cobalt-60** | **Cancer treatment (radiotherapy)**, **food irradiation**/sterilising |
| **Iodine-131** | **Thyroid** diagnosis and treatment |
| **Carbon-14** | **Age determination (dating)** |
| **Uranium-235**, Plutonium-239 | Nuclear fuel, bombs |
| Phosphorus-32 | Agriculture research, blood disorders |
| Technetium-99m | Medical imaging (most used diagnostic isotope) |
| Sodium-24 | Detecting blood clots / leaks in pipes |

## Nuclear fission and fusion 🔥🔥
| | **Fission (ফিশন/বিভাজন)** | **Fusion (ফিউশন/সংযোজন)** |
|---|---|---|
| What | A heavy nucleus **splits** into two lighter nuclei | Light nuclei **join** to form a heavier nucleus |
| Example | **U-235 + slow neutron → Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3 neutrons + ≈200 MeV** | **Hydrogen (deuterium + tritium) → Helium** + energy |
| Discovered | **Otto Hahn & Fritz Strassmann (1938)**; explained by Lise Meitner | Needs **millions of degrees** temperature |
| Where | **Atom bomb**, nuclear power plant | **Sun and stars**, **hydrogen bomb** |
| Energy per reaction | Large | **Much larger** per unit mass; little radioactive waste |

- The energy comes from **mass defect**, via **E = mc²** (Einstein).
- **Chain reaction**: neutrons released by fission split more nuclei. Uncontrolled → **atom bomb**; controlled → **reactor**.
- A hydrogen bomb needs a **fission bomb as a trigger** to reach the fusion temperature.
- **Hiroshima (6 August 1945)** — uranium bomb "Little Boy"; **Nagasaki (9 August 1945)** — plutonium bomb "Fat Man".

## Nuclear reactor (পারমাণবিক চুল্লি)
| Part | Material / job |
|---|---|
| **Fuel** | **Enriched uranium (U-235)**, or plutonium-239 |
| **Moderator** | **Heavy water (D₂O)** or **graphite** (also ordinary water) — **slows down neutrons** |
| **Control rods** | **Cadmium or boron** — **absorb neutrons** to control the reaction |
| **Coolant** | Water, heavy water, liquid sodium, CO₂ — carries heat away |
| **Shield** | Thick concrete/lead |

- First nuclear reactor: **Enrico Fermi, Chicago Pile-1 (1942)**.
- Major accidents: **Chernobyl (Ukraine, 1986)**, **Fukushima (Japan, 2011)**.
- **IAEA** (International Atomic Energy Agency): founded **1957**, HQ **Vienna**.

## Bangladesh and nuclear energy 🔥
- **Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission (BAEC)**: established **1973**.
- **Research reactor**: **TRIGA Mark-II, 3 MW**, at **AERE, Savar** — commissioned in **1986**.

SCI-09.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask states of matter, sublimation examples, physical vs chemical change, atomic models and their authors, electron configuration, and periodic-table facts (Mendeleev, groups, noble gases, most abundant elements, liquid elements).

## Matter and its states (পদার্থ ও তার অবস্থা) 🔥
- Matter has mass and occupies space. Three common states: **solid, liquid, gas**. **Plasma** is called the **4th state** (Sun, stars, lightning, neon sign). **Bose–Einstein condensate** is called the **5th state** (predicted by S. N. Bose & Einstein; made in 1995).
- **Sublimation (ঊর্ধ্বপাতন)**: solid → gas directly. Examples: **camphor (কর্পূর), naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl), dry ice (solid CO₂)**.
- **Physical change (ভৌত পরিবর্তন)**: no new substance, usually reversible — melting of ice, boiling water, dissolving salt/sugar, magnetising iron, making a solution.
- **Chemical change (রাসায়নিক পরিবর্তন)**: new substance forms — **rusting of iron, burning of paper/candle wax (burning), curdling of milk, digestion of food, photosynthesis, ripening of fruit**.
  - Candle burning shows both: melting wax (physical), burning wax (chemical).
- **Element (মৌল)**: one kind of atom. **Compound (যৌগ)**: elements combined in fixed ratio (water, salt). **Mixture (মিশ্রণ)**: no fixed ratio (air, sea water, soil, alloy like brass).

## Atomic models 🔥
| Model / idea | Scientist | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| "Atomos" (indivisible) | **Democritus** (Greek) | First idea of atoms |
| **Atomic theory (1803)** | **John Dalton** | Atoms are indivisible; elements combine in simple ratios |
| **Plum-pudding model** | **J. J. Thomson** (1904) | Electrons embedded in positive sphere |
| **Nuclear / solar-system model (1911)** | **Ernest Rutherford** | Tiny, dense, positive **nucleus**; most of the atom is empty space (gold-foil experiment) |
| **Bohr model (1913)** | **Niels Bohr** | Electrons move in **fixed orbits (energy levels)**; energy emitted/absorbed only when jumping between them |
| Quantum/wave model | Schrödinger, Heisenberg (uncertainty principle) | Orbitals |

- Rutherford's model failed to explain atomic **stability**; Bohr fixed this.
- **Electron configuration**: max electrons in a shell = **2n²** (K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32). Examples: Na (11) = 2, 8, 1; Cl (17) = 2, 8, 7; Ca (20) = 2, 8, 8, 2.
- **Valency (যোজনী)**: combining capacity, based on outer-shell electrons. **Noble gases have valency 0** (stable octet; helium has a duplet).
- **Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³** particles per **mole**. Molar volume of gas at STP = **22.4 litres**.
- **Ion**: charged atom — cation (+, lost electrons), anion (−, gained electrons).

## The periodic table (পর্যায় সারণি) 🔥🔥
| Step | Scientist |
|---|---|
| Law of triads | Döbereiner (1829) |
| Law of octaves | Newlands (1864) |
| **First periodic table (1869)**, based on **atomic mass**; left gaps for undiscovered elements | **Dmitri Mendeleev** (Russia) — **father of the periodic table** |
| **Modern periodic law (1913)**: properties depend on **atomic number** | **Henry Moseley** |

- **Modern table: 7 periods (horizontal rows, পর্যায়) and 18 groups (vertical columns, গ্রুপ)**. **118 elements** are known; about **92–94 occur naturally**.
- Newest elements (named 2016): **113 Nihonium (Nh), 115 Moscovium (Mc), 117 Tennessine (Ts), 118 Oganesson (Og)**.
- **Metals on the left**, **non-metals on the right**, **metalloids** along the zigzag line (**B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te**). **Lanthanides and actinides** are placed separately at the bottom (f-block).

| Group | Name | Members / facts |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Alkali metals** | Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr — very reactive, kept under **kerosene** |
| **2** | **Alkaline earth metals** | Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra |
| 3–12 | **Transition metals** | Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au, Hg … |
| **17** | **Halogens** ("salt-formers") | **F, Cl, Br, I, At** — **fluorine** is the most reactive non-metal and **most electronegative element** |
| **18** | **Noble / inert gases** | **He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn** — Rn is radioactive |

## Record-holding elements 🔥
| Fact | Element |
|---|---|
| **Most abundant in the universe**; lightest element | **Hydrogen** |
| **Most abundant in Earth's crust** | **Oxygen** (≈46%), then **silicon** |
| **Most abundant metal in the crust** | **Aluminium**, then iron |
| **Most abundant in the atmosphere** | **Nitrogen** (≈78%) |
| Most abundant in the human body (by mass) | **Oxygen**, then carbon |
| **Liquid at room temperature** | **Mercury** (metal) and **bromine** (non-metal) |
| **Lightest metal** | **Lithium** |
| **Densest element** | **Osmium** |
| **Hardest natural substance** | **Diamond** (a form of carbon) |
| **Best conductor** of electricity | Silver |
| Metal with lowest melting point | Mercury (−39 °C) |
| Highest melting point metal | Tungsten |

## Uses of noble gases
- **Helium**: filling balloons/airships (light, non-flammable); with O₂ for **deep-sea divers**; liquid He for cooling (MRI magnets).
- **Neon**: red advertising signs. **Argon**: filling electric bulbs, welding. **Xenon**: photographic flash, car headlamps. **Radon**: cancer radiotherapy (radioactive).

## Quick revision
- Plasma = **4th state**; BEC = 5th state (S. N. Bose).
- **Sublimation**: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, NH₄Cl, dry ice.
- **Rusting and burning are chemical changes**; melting and dissolving are physical.
- Nucleus: **Rutherford (1911)**; fixed orbits: **Bohr (1913)**; atomic theory: **Dalton (1803)**.
- Shell capacity **2n²**; Avogadro's number **6.022 × 10²³**.
- **Mendeleev (1869)** — atomic mass; **Moseley** — atomic number.
- **7 periods, 18 groups, 118 elements**; group 17 halogens, 18 noble gases.
- Liquid elements: **mercury and bromine**; crust: **O > Si > Al**.

SCI-10.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask "which acid is in lemon/vinegar/ant sting?", pH of blood and common liquids, indicator colours, strong acids with common names, aqua regia, and neutralisation in daily life.

## Acids, bases and alkalis 🔥
| Property | Acid (এসিড) | Base (ক্ষারক) |
|---|---|---|
| Taste / feel | **Sour (টক)** | **Bitter**, soapy/slippery |
| Ion in water (Arrhenius) | Gives **H⁺ (H₃O⁺)** | Gives **OH⁻** |
| Litmus | **Blue → red** | **Red → blue** |
| Phenolphthalein | Colourless | **Pink** |
| Methyl orange | **Red** | **Yellow** |
| pH | **Below 7** | **Above 7** |

- An **alkali (ক্ষার)** is a **water-soluble base** (NaOH, KOH). **All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis** (e.g. Cu(OH)₂ is insoluble).
- **Litmus** is obtained from **lichen**. Turmeric turns **reddish-brown** with a base.
- Other definitions: **Brønsted–Lowry** (acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor); **Lewis** (acid = electron-pair acceptor).

## Natural acids 🔥🔥
| Source | Acid |
|---|---|
| **Lemon, orange** (citrus) | **Citric acid** |
| **Vinegar (সিরকা)** | **Acetic acid** (≈ 5–8%) |
| **Sour milk, curd (দই)**; tired muscles | **Lactic acid** |
| **Tamarind (তেঁতুল)**, grapes | **Tartaric acid** |
| **Tomato**, spinach | **Oxalic acid** (tomato also has citric/malic) |
| **Apple** | **Malic acid** |
| **Ant sting, nettle sting (bee sting also often cited)** | **Formic acid** |
| **Tea** | **Tannic acid** |
| **Amla (আমলকী)**, citrus | **Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)** |
| **Gastric juice (stomach)** | **Hydrochloric acid (HCl)** |
| Urine | Uric acid |
| Rancid butter | Butyric acid |
| Proteins | Amino acids; fats → fatty acids |

## Strong acids and bases with common names 🔥
| Chemical | Formula | Common name / fact |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrochloric acid | HCl | **Muriatic acid**; in stomach |
| **Sulphuric acid** | **H₂SO₄** | **Oil of vitriol**, **"King of chemicals"**; made by **contact process**; car battery |
| Nitric acid | HNO₃ | Aqua fortis; fertilizer, explosives |
| **Aqua regia (অম্লরাজ)** | **3 HCl : 1 HNO₃** (by volume) | **Dissolves gold and platinum** |
| Hydrofluoric acid | HF | **Etches glass** (stored in plastic, not glass) |
| Carbonic acid | H₂CO₃ | In **soft drinks** (CO₂ dissolved) |
| Phenol | C₆H₅OH | **Carbolic acid**, antiseptic |
| Sodium hydroxide | NaOH | **Caustic soda** — soap making |
| Potassium hydroxide | KOH | **Caustic potash** — soft soap |
| Calcium hydroxide | Ca(OH)₂ | **Slaked lime (কলিচুন)**; its clear solution = **lime water** (turns milky with CO₂) |
| Magnesium hydroxide | Mg(OH)₂ | **Milk of magnesia** — **antacid**, laxative |
| Ammonium hydroxide | NH₄OH | Weak base; ammonia solution |

- **Acids + metals → salt + hydrogen gas**; acids + carbonates → CO₂.
- When diluting, **add acid to water, never water to acid** (the heat can make it splash).

## The pH scale 🔥🔥
- Introduced by **S. P. L. Sørensen (1909)**. **pH = −log[H⁺]**; scale usually **0 to 14**.
- **pH 7 = neutral** (pure water at 25 °C); **< 7 acidic**; **> 7 basic**. Each step = **10 times** change in H⁺ concentration.

| Substance | Approx. pH |
|---|---|
| **Gastric juice** | **1.5 – 3.5 (≈ 2)** |
| **Lemon juice** | **≈ 2.2 – 2.4** |
| Vinegar | ≈ 2.5 – 3 |
| Tomato juice | ≈ 4 – 4.5 |
| Black coffee | ≈ 5 |
| **Normal rain water** | **≈ 5.6** (CO₂ dissolved) |
| **Acid rain** | **Below 5.6** |
| **Milk** | **≈ 6.5 – 6.8** |
| Saliva | ≈ 6.5 – 7.4 |
| **Pure water** | **7** |
| **Human blood** | **7.35 – 7.45 (≈ 7.4), slightly alkaline** |
| Sea water | ≈ 8 |
| Baking soda solution | ≈ 8.3 |
| Milk of magnesia | ≈ 10.5 |
| Household ammonia | ≈ 11 – 12 |
| Lime water | ≈ 12.4 |
| Sodium hydroxide | ≈ 13 – 14 |

- Tooth enamel starts to decay when mouth pH falls **below about 5.5**; toothpaste is **basic**.
- Best soil pH for most crops ≈ **6 – 7.5**.

## Neutralisation and salts 🔥
- **Acid + base → salt + water** (neutralisation, প্রশমন). E.g. **HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O**.
- **Salt (লবণ)**: compound of the positive ion of a base and the negative ion of an acid. Types: normal (NaCl), **acid salt (NaHSO₄, NaHCO₃)**, basic salt.

| Daily-life use | How |
|---|---|
| **Acidity / indigestion** | **Antacid** — milk of magnesia, **baking soda**, Al(OH)₃ |
| **Ant or bee sting** (acidic) | Rub **baking soda** or a mild base |
| Wasp sting (alkaline) | Vinegar |
| **Acidic soil** | Add **lime (CaO / Ca(OH)₂) or chalk** |
| Alkaline soil | Add **gypsum**, organic matter |
| Factory acid waste | Neutralised with slaked lime |

- **Acid rain** comes from **SO₂ and NOₓ**; it damages **marble (CaCO₃)** buildings (e.g. the Taj Mahal's "marble cancer"), soil and fish.

## Quick revision
- Acid: sour, **blue litmus → red**, pH < 7; base: bitter, red → blue, pH > 7.
- Lemon **citric**, vinegar **acetic**, curd **lactic**, tamarind **tartaric**, ant **formic**, tomato **oxalic**, tea **tannic**, stomach **HCl**.
- **Blood pH ≈ 7.4** (slightly alkaline); pure water **7**; gastric juice ≈ 2.
- Normal rain ≈ **5.6**; acid rain below that (SO₂, NOₓ).
- **Aqua regia = 3 HCl : 1 HNO₃** — dissolves gold.
- **H₂SO₄ = king of chemicals**; NaOH = caustic soda; Mg(OH)₂ = milk of magnesia.
- Phenolphthalein turns **pink in base**; methyl orange red in acid.
- pH scale: **Sørensen (1909)**.

SCI-11.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Alloy-composition and ore-name tables are among the most repeated chemistry questions. Exams also ask rust prevention (galvanising), exceptions among metals/non-metals and the reactivity series.

## Metals vs non-metals 🔥
| Metals (ধাতু) | Non-metals (অধাতু) |
|---|---|
| Lustrous, **malleable** (sheets) and **ductile** (wires) | Brittle, dull (mostly) |
| Good conductors of heat and electricity | Poor conductors |
| Lose electrons → positive ions; oxides are basic | Gain electrons; oxides are acidic |

**Exceptions (asked often):**
- **Mercury** is a metal but **liquid** at room temperature.
- **Sodium and potassium** are **soft** (cut with a knife), light, and kept **under kerosene** (react violently with water/air).
- **Graphite** (non-metal, carbon) **conducts electricity**; used in electrodes and pencils.
- **Iodine** (non-metal) is **lustrous**. **Diamond** (non-metal) is the **hardest natural substance**.
- **Gold** is the most **malleable and ductile** metal; **silver** the best conductor; **tungsten** has the highest melting point.
- **Gold and platinum** occur **free (native)** in nature because they are very unreactive (noble metals).
- **Iron** is the **most used** metal; **aluminium** is the most abundant metal in the crust.

## Reactivity series (সক্রিয়তা সিরিজ)
**K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt**
- Metals above hydrogen displace H₂ from dilute acids. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt (e.g. **iron displaces copper** from CuSO₄ solution).

## Alloys (সংকর ধাতু) 🔥🔥
| Alloy | Composition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Brass (পিতল)** | **Copper + Zinc** | Utensils, fittings, cartridges |
| **Bronze (কাঁসা/ব্রোঞ্জ)** | **Copper + Tin** | Statues, medals, utensils |
| **Bell metal** | Copper + Tin (more tin, ≈ 78:22) | Bells, plates (a type of bronze) |
| **Gun metal** | Copper + Tin + Zinc | Gun parts, gears |
| **German silver** | **Copper + Zinc + Nickel** (**no silver**) | Utensils, ornaments |
| **Steel (ইস্পাত)** | **Iron + Carbon** (≈ 0.1–1.5% C) | Construction, tools |
| **Stainless steel** | **Iron + Chromium + Nickel** (+ C) | Rust-proof cutlery, utensils, surgical tools |
| **Solder (ঝালাই)** | **Lead + Tin** | Joining electrical wires |
| **Duralumin** | **Aluminium + Copper** + Mg + Mn | **Aircraft bodies** (light, strong) |
| **Magnalium** | Aluminium + Magnesium | Aircraft parts, balances |
| **Nichrome** | Nickel + Chromium | **Heater coils** |
| **Invar** | Iron + Nickel | Clock pendulums, measuring tapes (low expansion) |
| **Alnico** | Aluminium + Nickel + Cobalt (+ Fe) | Permanent magnets |
| **Amalgam** | **Mercury + another metal** | Dental filling (silver-tin amalgam) |
| Type metal | Lead + Antimony + Tin | Printing type |
| **22-carat gold (গিনি সোনা)** | 22 parts gold + 2 parts copper (≈ 91.6% gold) | Jewellery; **24 carat = pure gold** |

## Ores (আকরিক) 🔥🔥
A **mineral** is a naturally occurring compound; an **ore** is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably. All ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores.

| Metal | Main ore(s) |
|---|---|
| **Aluminium** | **Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O)**; cryolite used in extraction |
| **Iron** | **Haematite (Fe₂O₃)** (main), **magnetite (Fe₃O₄)**, limonite, siderite (FeCO₃) |
| **Copper** | **Chalcopyrite / copper pyrites (CuFeS₂)**, cuprite, malachite |
| **Zinc** | **Zinc blende (ZnS)**, calamine (ZnCO₃) |
| **Lead** | **Galena (PbS)** |
| **Mercury** | **Cinnabar (HgS)** |
| **Tin** | **Cassiterite / tinstone (SnO₂)** |
| **Manganese** | Pyrolusite (MnO₂) |
| **Uranium** | **Pitchblende** |
| Sodium | Rock salt (NaCl) |
| Calcium | Limestone (CaCO₃), **gypsum** |
| Magnesium | Dolomite, magnesite, carnallite |

- **Aluminium** is extracted by **electrolysis** of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite (Hall–Héroult process).
- **Iron** is extracted in a **blast furnace** using **coke** and **limestone**. **Pig iron** has the most carbon (≈ 4%); **wrought iron** is the purest (least carbon).

## Corrosion 🔥
- **Rusting of iron** needs **both oxygen (air) and water (moisture)**; rust is **hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O**. Salt water speeds it up.
- Prevention: **galvanising** (coating with **zinc**), painting, oiling/greasing, **tin plating** (tin cans), alloying (stainless steel), electroplating (chromium).
- **Copper** gets a green coat (**verdigris**, basic copper carbonate). **Silver** turns black (**silver sulphide, Ag₂S**). Gold does not corrode.

## Metals in life and pollution
| Metal | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Iron** | In **haemoglobin** |
| **Magnesium** | In **chlorophyll** |
| **Cobalt** | In **vitamin B₁₂** |
| **Arsenic** | **Groundwater contamination in Bangladesh**; arsenicosis (skin lesions) |
| **Mercury** | **Minamata disease** (Japan) |
| **Cadmium** | **Itai-itai disease** (Japan) |
| **Lead** | Damages brain/nerves, especially in children |

## Bangladesh minerals (quick facts)
- **Hard rock (granite): Maddhapara, Dinajpur**. **Coal: Barapukuria (Dinajpur)** (only coal mine in production), also Phulbari, Khalashpir, Jamalganj, Dighipara.
- **Limestone**: Takerghat (Sunamganj), Joypurhat. **White clay**: Bijoypur (Netrokona). **Heavy mineral sand** (zircon, ilmenite, rutile, monazite): Cox's Bazar coast.
- **Iron ore**: discovered at **Isabpur, Hakimpur (Dinajpur)** in **2019** by the Geological Survey of Bangladesh.

## Quick revision
- **Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn**; German silver = Cu + Zn + Ni (no silver).
- **Stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni**; solder = Pb + Sn; duralumin for aircraft.
- **Amalgam** = mercury alloy; 24-carat gold is pure; 22-carat has copper.
- **Bauxite → Al; haematite → Fe; galena → Pb; cinnabar → Hg; cassiterite → Sn; zinc blende → Zn**.
- Rust = **Fe₂O₃·xH₂O**; needs air + water; **galvanising = zinc coating**.
- Mercury: liquid metal; graphite: conducting non-metal; Na/K kept in kerosene.
- Most abundant metal in crust: **aluminium**; most used: **iron**.

SCI-12.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask allotropes of carbon, main component of natural gas/LPG/biogas, which gas ripens fruit, natural vs synthetic polymers (nylon, PVC, Teflon, Bakelite), coal types, petroleum fractions and octane number.

## Carbon and its allotropes (কার্বনের রূপভেদ) 🔥
- Carbon forms long chains and rings with itself (**catenation**), so it has millions of compounds. **Organic chemistry = chemistry of carbon compounds**.
- **Friedrich Wöhler (1828)** made **urea** in the laboratory (from ammonium cyanate), ending the "vital force" theory; he is called the father of organic chemistry.

| Allotrope | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Diamond** | **Hardest natural substance**; each C bonded to 4 others (tetrahedral); **bad conductor**; cuts glass |
| **Graphite** | Soft, slippery layers; **conducts electricity**; pencil "lead", lubricant, electrodes, moderator in reactors |
| **Fullerene (C₆₀, buckyball)** | Discovered **1985** (Kroto, Curl, Smalley — Nobel 1996) |
| **Graphene** | Single layer of graphite; isolated **2004** by **Geim & Novoselov** (Nobel Physics 2010) |
| **Carbon nanotube** | Reported by **Sumio Iijima (1991)** |
| Amorphous forms | Coal, charcoal, coke, **lampblack/soot**, animal charcoal (bone black; used to decolourise sugar) |

## Hydrocarbons and important compounds 🔥
| Compound | Formula | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Methane** | **CH₄** | **Marsh gas**; main component of **natural gas** (≈ 95%+ in Bangladesh gas), **biogas** (≈ 55–70%) and **CNG** |
| Ethane | C₂H₆ | Alkane |
| **Propane + butane** | C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀ | **LPG (liquefied petroleum gas)**; a smelly compound (**ethyl mercaptan**) is added to detect leaks |
| **Ethylene (ethene)** | **C₂H₄** | **Natural fruit-ripening hormone/gas**; makes polythene |
| **Acetylene (ethyne)** | **C₂H₂** | **Oxy-acetylene welding**; produced from **calcium carbide (CaC₂)**, which is **illegally used to ripen fruit** (harmful) |
| **Methanol** | CH₃OH | **Wood spirit**; **poisonous** — can cause **blindness** and death |
| **Ethanol** | C₂H₅OH | Drinking alcohol; made by **fermentation** of molasses/sugar by **yeast**; rectified spirit ≈ 95%, absolute alcohol 100%; **methylated/denatured spirit** = ethanol + methanol |
| **Formaldehyde** | HCHO | **Formalin = 37–40% solution**; preserves biological specimens; **illegal in food** |
| **Benzene** | C₆H₆ | Ring structure proposed by **Kekulé** |
| Chloroform | CHCl₃ | Early anaesthetic |
| Glycerol | C₃H₈O₃ | From fats; used in cosmetics, explosives (nitroglycerine) |

## Polymers (পলিমার) 🔥🔥
A polymer is a giant molecule made of repeating units (**monomers**).

| Natural polymers | Monomer |
|---|---|
| **Starch, cellulose, glycogen** | **Glucose** |
| **Protein** (silk, wool, hair) | **Amino acids** |
| **Natural rubber** | **Isoprene** |
| DNA / RNA | Nucleotides |

| Synthetic polymer | Monomer / fact | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Polythene (polyethylene)** | **Ethylene** | Bags, bottles |
| **PVC (polyvinyl chloride)** | **Vinyl chloride** | **Pipes**, raincoats, wire insulation |
| **Teflon (PTFE)** | Tetrafluoroethylene | **Non-stick cookware** |
| **Nylon** | **First fully synthetic fibre**, **Wallace Carothers (DuPont), 1935** | Ropes, parachutes, fishing nets |
| **Polyester (terylene/dacron)** | — | Clothing |
| **Bakelite** | **First synthetic plastic, Leo Baekeland (1907)**; **thermosetting** | Electrical switches, handles |
| Melamine | Thermosetting | Crockery |
| Polystyrene | Styrene | Packaging foam (thermocol) |
| Acrylic (PMMA / Perspex) | — | Sheets, "artificial wool" (acrylic fibre) |
| Rayon | **Artificial silk**, made from cellulose (semi-synthetic) | Textiles |

- **Thermoplastics** soften on heating and can be remoulded (polythene, PVC). **Thermosetting plastics** set permanently (Bakelite, melamine).
- **Vulcanisation**: heating rubber with **sulphur** to make it hard and elastic — **Charles Goodyear (1839)**.
- **Bangladesh banned polythene shopping bags in 2002** (among the first countries). **"Sonali bag"**: a biodegradable jute-cellulose bag developed by scientist **Dr. Mubarak Ahmad Khan**.

## Fuels (জ্বালানি) 🔥
- **Fossil fuels**: **coal, petroleum, natural gas** — formed from buried plants/animals over millions of years; non-renewable.

| Coal type | Carbon content |
|---|---|
| **Peat** | Lowest (first stage) |
| **Lignite (brown coal)** | Low |
| **Bituminous** | Medium–high (most common; Barapukuria coal is bituminous) |
| **Anthracite** | **Highest (≈ 90%+)**, best quality |

**Petroleum (crude oil, খনিজ তেল)** is separated by **fractional distillation**. Fractions from top (low boiling point) to bottom: **refinery gas/LPG → petrol (gasoline) → kerosene (jet fuel) → diesel → lubricating oil → paraffin wax → bitumen (asphalt, for roads)**.

- **Octane number** measures **petrol quality** (resistance to **knocking**); **cetane number** measures diesel quality. **Tetraethyl lead** was an anti-knock agent (now banned due to lead pollution).
- **Calorific value**: heat per unit mass. **Hydrogen has the highest calorific value** (≈ 150 kJ/g) and burns clean (product: water).
- Gas mixtures: **water gas = CO + H₂**; **producer gas = CO + N₂**; **coal gas** = H₂ + CH₄ + CO.
- **Natural gas in Bangladesh**: first discovered at **Haripur, Sylhet (1955)**. It is the **main commercial energy source** and used for power, fertilizer (urea), CNG and cooking.
- **Carbon monoxide (CO)** from incomplete burning is **poisonous**: it binds **haemoglobin** more strongly than oxygen.

## Fire safety
- Fire needs **fuel, heat and oxygen** (fire triangle).
- **CO₂ extinguishers** cut off oxygen. **Do not use water on oil or electrical fires** — use **foam, CO₂ or dry powder**.

## Quick revision
- **Diamond hardest, non-conductor; graphite conducts**; fullerene C₆₀; graphene 2004.
- Natural gas, biogas, CNG: mainly **methane (CH₄)**; LPG: **propane + butane**.
- **Ethylene ripens fruit**; **calcium carbide** (acetylene) illegally used for ripening.
- Methanol poisonous (blindness); ethanol by yeast fermentation; formalin = 37–40% HCHO.
- **Nylon: first synthetic fibre (Carothers)**; **Bakelite: first synthetic plastic**; **Teflon: non-stick**; PVC: pipes.
- **Vulcanisation = rubber + sulphur** (Goodyear).
- Coal: **anthracite best**, peat lowest; octane number = petrol quality.
- Wöhler synthesised **urea (1828)**.

## Fertilizers (সার) 🔥
- **Primary plant nutrients: N, P, K** (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium).

| Fertilizer | Nutrient | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Urea — CO(NH₂)₂** | **Nitrogen (≈ 46% N)** | **Most used fertilizer in Bangladesh**; made from **natural gas** (ammonia + CO₂) |
| **TSP (triple super phosphate)** | **Phosphorus** | |
| **MoP (muriate of potash, KCl)** | **Potassium** | |
| **DAP (diammonium phosphate)** | **N + P** | |
| Ammonium sulphate | N + S | |
| **Gypsum** | **Sulphur** (+ calcium) | |
| **Zinc sulphate** | **Zinc** | Zinc deficiency causes "khaira" disease of rice |
| Compost, cow dung, vermicompost | Organic | Improves soil structure |

- **Ammonia (NH₃)** is made by the **Haber (Haber–Bosch) process** (N₂ + 3H₂, iron catalyst). **Sulphuric acid** by the **contact process**.
- Urea factories in Bangladesh include **Ghorasal–Palash (Narsingdi)**, **Jamuna (Sarishabari, Jamalpur)**, **Shahjalal (Fenchuganj, Sylhet)**, Ashuganj, **KAFCO** and Chittagong Urea (Chattogram).
- Nitrogen deficiency → leaves turn **yellow**; nitrogen-fixing bacteria (**Rhizobium**) live in legume root nodules.

## Soap, detergent and hard water 🔥
- **Soap = sodium or potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids**. Made by **saponification (সাবানায়ন)**: **fat/oil + NaOH (or KOH) → soap + glycerol**.
- **Sodium soap = hard soap** (washing); **potassium soap = soft soap** (shaving cream, liquid soap).
- Soap molecule has a water-loving (hydrophilic) head and oil-loving (hydrophobic) tail → forms **micelles** that remove grease.
- **Hard water** contains **Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺** salts; soap forms **scum** and does not lather.
  - **Temporary hardness**: bicarbonates of Ca/Mg — removed by **boiling** (or Clark's method, adding lime).
  - **Permanent hardness**: chlorides/sulphates of Ca/Mg — removed by **washing soda**, ion-exchange (permutit).
- **Detergents** (sulphonates) work well even in **hard water**; some are non-biodegradable and pollute water.

## Glass (কাচ) 🔥
- Glass is an **amorphous solid / super-cooled liquid** (no fixed melting point).
- **Ordinary (soda-lime) glass**: **sand (SiO₂) + soda ash (Na₂CO₃) + limestone (CaCO₃)** melted together.

| Type | Special ingredient / use |
|---|---|
| **Pyrex (borosilicate)** | Boron oxide; **heat-resistant** lab ware, ovenware |
| **Flint / crystal (lead) glass** | Lead oxide; lenses, prisms, decorative crystal |
| Photochromic glass | Silver halide; sunglasses that darken in sunlight |
| Safety / bullet-proof glass | Layers of glass and plastic |
| Optical fibre | Very pure silica glass |

| Colouring agent | Colour of glass |

| **Cobalt oxide** | **Blue** |
| **Chromium oxide** | **Green** |
| **Manganese dioxide** | **Purple / violet** |
| **Gold (chloride)** | **Ruby red** |
| Cuprous oxide | Red |

- Glass is **etched by hydrofluoric acid (HF)**.

## Cement and construction 🔥
- **Portland cement** was invented by **Joseph Aspdin (England, 1824)**; set cement looked like Portland stone.
- Raw materials: **limestone + clay** (heated to form "clinker"); **gypsum** is added to **slow down setting**.
- Main compounds: calcium silicates and calcium aluminate.
- **Mortar** = cement + sand + water. **Concrete** = cement + sand + gravel/stone chips + water. **RCC** = concrete reinforced with steel rods.
- Cement sets by **hydration** (reaction with water); curing (keeping it wet) makes it strong.
- **Chhatak Cement Factory (Sunamganj)** is the oldest cement factory in Bangladesh.

## Other everyday chemistry
- **Gunpowder**: potassium nitrate + sulphur + charcoal (≈ 75 : 10 : 15).
- **Dynamite**: **Alfred Nobel (1867)**, based on **nitroglycerine**. TNT = trinitrotoluene.
- Matchbox side has **red phosphorus**; match head has potassium chlorate and antimony trisulphide.
- Photography uses **silver bromide (AgBr)**. Mirror backing: silver (now often aluminium).
- Fluoride in toothpaste prevents tooth decay.

SCI-14.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask who discovered the cell and nucleus, the "powerhouse"/"suicide bag" of the cell, plant vs animal cell, mitosis vs meiosis, and types of plant and animal tissues (xylem/phloem, tendon/ligament).

## Discovery of the cell 🔥
| Discovery | Scientist |
|---|---|
| **Cell (dead cork cells), 1665**, book *Micrographia* | **Robert Hooke** |
| First to see **living cells** (bacteria, protozoa), 1670s | **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** (father of microbiology) |
| **Nucleus (1831)** | **Robert Brown** |
| **Cell theory (1838–39)** | **Schleiden** (plants) and **Schwann** (animals) |
| "All cells come from pre-existing cells" (1855) | **Rudolf Virchow** |
| Term "protoplasm" | Purkinje |

- The cell is the **structural and functional unit of life**.
- **Largest cell: ostrich egg**. **Smallest cell: Mycoplasma (PPLO)**. **Longest human cell: neuron (nerve cell)**. **Largest human cell: ovum**; the **sperm** is usually cited as the smallest human cell.
- **Mature mammalian RBCs have no nucleus**.

## Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells
| Prokaryotic (আদিকোষ) | Eukaryotic (প্রকৃতকোষ) |
|---|---|
| **No true nucleus** (no nuclear membrane) | True nucleus with membrane |
| No membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, chloroplast) | Has them |
| Examples: **bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria)** | Plants, animals, fungi, protozoa |

## Cell organelles (কোষ অঙ্গাণু) 🔥🔥
| Organelle | Function / nickname |
|---|---|
| **Nucleus** | **Control centre**; contains **chromosomes (DNA)**; nucleolus makes ribosomes |
| **Mitochondria** | **"Powerhouse of the cell"**; aerobic respiration (**Krebs cycle**), makes **ATP**; has its own DNA |
| **Chloroplast** | **Photosynthesis** ("kitchen of the cell"); contains **chlorophyll**; only in plants/algae; has its own DNA |
| **Ribosome** | **Protein synthesis**; no membrane; found in all cells |
| Endoplasmic reticulum | Transport; rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins, smooth ER makes lipids |
| **Golgi apparatus** (Camillo Golgi) | **Packaging and secretion**; forms lysosomes |
| **Lysosome** | **"Suicide bag"**; digestive enzymes (discovered by **Christian de Duve**) |
| **Centrosome / centriole** | Helps **cell division** (spindle); mainly in **animal cells** |
| **Vacuole** | Stores cell sap; **large and central in plant cells** |
| **Plasma (cell) membrane** | **Selectively (semi-) permeable**; controls entry and exit |
| **Cell wall** | Rigid outer layer: **cellulose in plants**, **chitin in fungi**, peptidoglycan in bacteria |

### Plant cell vs animal cell 🔥
| Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|
| **Cell wall present** (cellulose) | Absent |
| **Chloroplast present** | Absent |
| **Large central vacuole** | Small/temporary vacuoles |
| Centrosome usually absent | **Centrosome present** |
| Stores food as **starch** | Stores food as **glycogen** |

## Cell division (কোষ বিভাজন) 🔥
| | **Mitosis (মাইটোসিস)** | **Meiosis (মিয়োসিস)** |
|---|---|---|
| Where | **Somatic (body) cells**; growth, repair | **Reproductive cells** (to form **gametes**: sperm, egg) |
| Daughter cells | **2**, identical to parent | **4**, different |
| Chromosome number | **Same** (2n → 2n) | **Halved (2n → n)** — "reduction division" |
| Stages | Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase | Two divisions (Meiosis I & II); crossing over |

- The term **mitosis** was given by **Walther Flemming**. **Amitosis** (direct division) occurs in bacteria/yeast.
- **Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs)** in body cells; **gametes have 23**.
- Uncontrolled mitosis leads to **cancer**.
- **Diffusion**: movement of molecules from high to low concentration. **Osmosis (অভিস্রবণ)**: movement of **water** through a semi-permeable membrane from **dilute to concentrated** solution (root hairs absorb water by osmosis; raisins swell in water; salted vegetables shrink).

## Tissue (টিস্যু/কলা) 🔥
A **tissue** is a group of similar cells doing a common function. **Histology** is the study of tissues; **Marcello Malpighi** is called the father of histology (the word "tissue" was popularised by Bichat).

### Plant tissues
| Type | Kind | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Meristematic (ভাজক)** | Dividing cells at **root and shoot tips** | Growth in length/girth |
| **Parenchyma** | Simple permanent | Storage, photosynthesis |
| **Collenchyma** | Simple permanent | Flexibility, mechanical support in young stems |
| **Sclerenchyma** | Simple permanent, dead thick-walled | Strength (fibres of **jute**, coconut husk) |
| **Xylem (জাইলেম)** | Complex | Carries **water and minerals upward** from roots; wood is xylem |
| **Phloem (ফ্লোয়েম)** | Complex | Carries **food (sugar)** from leaves to all parts |

- **Jute fibre** comes from the **phloem (bast) fibres** of the jute stem.

### Animal tissues
| Type | Examples / fact |
|---|---|
| **Epithelial (আবরণী)** | Skin surface, lining of gut; protection, secretion, absorption |
| **Connective (যোজক)** | **Bone, cartilage, blood (a fluid connective tissue)**, fat (adipose), **tendon** and **ligament** |
| **Muscular (পেশি)** | **Striated/skeletal (voluntary)**, **smooth (involuntary**, stomach, intestine, blood vessels), **cardiac** (heart; involuntary, striated, never tires) |
| **Nervous (স্নায়ু)** | **Neuron** — carries impulses; longest cell |

- **Tendon** joins **muscle to bone**. **Ligament** joins **bone to bone**.
- **Stem cells** are unspecialised cells that can become many cell types (bone marrow, umbilical cord blood).

## Quick revision
- **Robert Hooke (1665)** discovered the cell; **Robert Brown (1831)** the nucleus.
- Cell theory: **Schleiden & Schwann**; "omnis cellula e cellula": Virchow.
- **Mitochondria = powerhouse** (ATP); **lysosome = suicide bag**; ribosome = protein synthesis.
- Plant cell has **cell wall (cellulose), chloroplast, large vacuole**; animal cell has centrosome.
- **Mitosis → 2 identical cells; meiosis → 4 cells with half chromosomes**.
- Humans: **46 chromosomes**; gametes 23.
- **Xylem carries water; phloem carries food**.
- **Tendon: muscle–bone; ligament: bone–bone**; blood is connective tissue.
- Largest cell ostrich egg; longest human cell neuron; bacteria are prokaryotes.
